\textbf{\LARGE Infinite Series Worksheet (9.3) --- Solutions}

\vspace{10pt}

\typehead{Type A: Geometric Series}{A geometric series has the form
$$
a + ar + ar^2 + \cdots + ar^{k-1} + \cdots,
$$
where each term is obtained by multiplying the previous term by the same number $r$.

\textbf{How to find $a$ and $r$:}
\begin{itemize}
\item[\textbf{1.}] $a$ = \textbf{the first term} of the series. Plug in the \emph{starting} value of $k$ (which may be $k=0$, $k=1$, $k=2$, \dots).
\item[\textbf{2.}] $r$ = \textbf{(second term)} $\div$ \textbf{(first term)}. To be sure the series is geometric, also check that the ratio of \emph{any} two consecutive terms, $\dfrac{u_{k+1}}{u_k}$, is the same constant $r$.
\item[\textbf{3.}] If $|r| < 1$, the series converges and its sum is $\dfrac{a}{1-r}$. If $|r| \ge 1$, the series diverges.
\end{itemize}}

\problem{1.}{\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{7}{3^{k}} = 7 + \frac{7}{3} + \frac{7}{3^{2}} + \cdots + \frac{7}{3^{k}} + \cdots}

\step{Find $a$.} The series starts at $k = 0$, so the first term is
$$
a = \frac{7}{3^{0}} = \frac{7}{1} = 7.
$$

\step{Find $r$.} The second term ($k=1$) is $\dfrac{7}{3}$, so
$$
r = \frac{\text{second term}}{\text{first term}} = \frac{7/3}{7} = \frac{1}{3}.
$$
Check with the general term: $\dfrac{u_{k+1}}{u_k} = \dfrac{7/3^{k+1}}{7/3^{k}} = \dfrac{3^{k}}{3^{k+1}} = \dfrac13$ for every $k$. $\checkmark$

\step{Converge or diverge?} $|r| = \frac13 < 1$, so the series converges and
$$
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{7}{3^{k}} = \frac{a}{1-r} = \frac{7}{1-\frac13} = \frac{7}{\frac23} = 7\cdot\frac32 = \frac{21}{2}.
$$
\answer{converges, sum $= \dfrac{21}{2}$}

\problem{2.}{\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{k}\, 6}{5^{k}} = 6 - \frac{6}{5} + \frac{6}{5^{2}} - \cdots + \frac{(-1)^{k}\,6}{5^{k}} + \cdots}

\step{Find $a$.} The series starts at $k = 0$:
$$
a = \frac{(-1)^{0}\cdot 6}{5^{0}} = \frac{1\cdot 6}{1} = 6.
$$

\step{Find $r$.} The second term ($k=1$) is $\dfrac{(-1)^1\cdot 6}{5} = -\dfrac65$, so
$$
r = \frac{-6/5}{6} = -\frac{1}{5}.
$$
Check: $\dfrac{u_{k+1}}{u_k} = \dfrac{(-1)^{k+1}\,6/5^{k+1}}{(-1)^{k}\,6/5^{k}} = (-1)\cdot\dfrac{5^k}{5^{k+1}} = -\dfrac15$. $\checkmark$ \newline
(The alternating signs give a \emph{negative} ratio.)

\step{Converge or diverge?} $|r| = \frac15 < 1$, so the series converges and
$$
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{k}\, 6}{5^{k}} = \frac{a}{1-r} = \frac{6}{1-\left(-\frac15\right)} = \frac{6}{\frac65} = 5.
$$
\answer{converges, sum $= 5$}

\problem{3.}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 2^{2k}\, 3^{1-k} = 4 + \frac{16}{3} + \frac{64}{9} + \cdots + 2^{2k}\,3^{1-k} + \cdots}

\step{Find $a$.} The series starts at $k = 1$:
$$
a = 2^{2(1)}\cdot 3^{1-1} = 2^{2}\cdot 3^{0} = 4\cdot 1 = 4.
$$

\step{Find $r$.} The second term ($k=2$) is $2^{4}\cdot 3^{-1} = \dfrac{16}{3}$, so
$$
r = \frac{16/3}{4} = \frac{16}{12} = \frac{4}{3}.
$$
Check (concealed form): $2^{2k}\,3^{1-k} = \dfrac{4^{k}}{3^{k-1}} = 4\cdot\dfrac{4^{k-1}}{3^{k-1}} = 4\left(\dfrac43\right)^{k-1}$, which is $ar^{k-1}$ with $a=4$, $r=\frac43$. $\checkmark$

\step{Converge or diverge?} $|r| = \frac43 \ge 1$, so the series diverges.
\answer{diverges}

\problem{4.}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{5^{k+1}}{8^{k}} = \frac{25}{8} + \frac{125}{64} + \frac{625}{512} + \cdots + \frac{5^{k+1}}{8^{k}} + \cdots}

\step{Find $a$.} The series starts at $k = 1$:
$$
a = \frac{5^{1+1}}{8^{1}} = \frac{25}{8}.
$$

\step{Find $r$.} The second term ($k=2$) is $\dfrac{5^{3}}{8^{2}} = \dfrac{125}{64}$, so
$$
r = \frac{125/64}{25/8} = \frac{125}{64}\cdot\frac{8}{25} = \frac{5}{8}.
$$
Check: $\dfrac{u_{k+1}}{u_k} = \dfrac{5^{k+2}/8^{k+1}}{5^{k+1}/8^{k}} = \dfrac{5^{k+2}}{5^{k+1}}\cdot\dfrac{8^{k}}{8^{k+1}} = 5\cdot\dfrac18 = \dfrac58$. $\checkmark$

\step{Converge or diverge?} $|r| = \frac58 < 1$, so the series converges and
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{5^{k+1}}{8^{k}} = \frac{a}{1-r} = \frac{\frac{25}{8}}{1-\frac58} = \frac{\frac{25}{8}}{\frac38} = \frac{25}{3}.
$$
\answer{converges, sum $= \dfrac{25}{3}$}

\problem{5.}{\sum_{k=2}^{\infty} \frac{3^{k}}{2^{3k-1}} = \frac{9}{32} + \frac{27}{256} + \frac{81}{2048} + \cdots + \frac{3^{k}}{2^{3k-1}} + \cdots}

\step{Find $a$.} Careful: this series starts at $k = 2$, so the first term is
$$
a = \frac{3^{2}}{2^{3(2)-1}} = \frac{9}{2^{5}} = \frac{9}{32}.
$$
(A common mistake is to use $k=1$ or $k=0$ here.)

\step{Find $r$.} The second term ($k=3$) is $\dfrac{3^{3}}{2^{8}} = \dfrac{27}{256}$, so
$$
r = \frac{27/256}{9/32} = \frac{27}{256}\cdot\frac{32}{9} = \frac{3}{8}.
$$
Check: $\dfrac{u_{k+1}}{u_k} = \dfrac{3^{k+1}/2^{3k+2}}{3^{k}/2^{3k-1}} = \dfrac{3^{k+1}}{3^{k}}\cdot\dfrac{2^{3k-1}}{2^{3k+2}} = 3\cdot\dfrac{1}{2^{3}} = \dfrac38$. $\checkmark$

\step{Converge or diverge?} $|r| = \frac38 < 1$, so the series converges and
$$
\sum_{k=2}^{\infty} \frac{3^{k}}{2^{3k-1}} = \frac{a}{1-r} = \frac{\frac{9}{32}}{1-\frac38} = \frac{\frac{9}{32}}{\frac58} = \frac{9}{32}\cdot\frac{8}{5} = \frac{9}{20}.
$$
\answer{converges, sum $= \dfrac{9}{20}$}

\problem{6.}{3 + \frac{3}{4} + \frac{3}{4^{2}} + \cdots + \frac{3}{4^{k-1}} + \cdots}

\step{Find $a$.} Read the first term directly from the list: $a = 3$. \newline
(In sigma notation the series is $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{3}{4^{k-1}}$, and $k=1$ gives $\frac{3}{4^0} = 3$.)

\step{Find $r$.} The second term is $\dfrac34$, so
$$
r = \frac{3/4}{3} = \frac{1}{4}.
$$
Check: $\dfrac{3}{4^{k-1}} = 3\left(\dfrac14\right)^{k-1}$, which is $ar^{k-1}$ with $a=3$, $r = \frac14$. $\checkmark$

\step{Converge or diverge?} $|r| = \frac14 < 1$, so the series converges and
$$
\frac{a}{1-r} = \frac{3}{1-\frac14} = \frac{3}{\frac34} = 4.
$$
\answer{converges, sum $= 4$}

\problem{7.}{\frac{2}{9} - \frac{4}{27} + \frac{8}{81} - \cdots + \frac{(-1)^{k-1}\,2^{k}}{3^{k+1}} + \cdots}

\step{Find $a$.} Read the first term directly: $a = \dfrac29$. \newline
(With the general term starting at $k=1$: $\frac{(-1)^{0}\,2^{1}}{3^{2}} = \frac29$.)

\step{Find $r$.} The second term is $-\dfrac{4}{27}$, so
$$
r = \frac{-4/27}{2/9} = -\frac{4}{27}\cdot\frac{9}{2} = -\frac{2}{3}.
$$
Check with the third term: $\dfrac{8/81}{-4/27} = \dfrac{8}{81}\cdot\left(-\dfrac{27}{4}\right) = -\dfrac23$. $\checkmark$ \newline
In general, $\dfrac{(-1)^{k-1}\,2^{k}}{3^{k+1}} = \dfrac{2}{9}\left(-\dfrac23\right)^{k-1}$.

\step{Converge or diverge?} $|r| = \frac23 < 1$, so the series converges and
$$
\frac{a}{1-r} = \frac{\frac29}{1-\left(-\frac23\right)} = \frac{\frac29}{\frac53} = \frac29\cdot\frac35 = \frac{2}{15}.
$$
\answer{converges, sum $= \dfrac{2}{15}$}

\newpage

\typehead{Type B: Telescoping Sums}{\textbf{Method:} (1) Use partial fractions (or log rules) to write each term as a difference $u_k = b_k - b_{k+m}$. (2) Write out $s_n$ and cancel the inner terms to get a closed form. (3) The sum of the series is $\lim_{n\to+\infty} s_n$; if the limit does not exist, the series diverges.}

\problem{8.}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k^{2}+3k+2} = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{20} + \cdots + \frac{1}{k^{2}+3k+2} + \cdots}

\step{Partial fractions.} $k^2 + 3k + 2 = (k+1)(k+2)$, and
$$
\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)} = \frac{1}{k+1} - \frac{1}{k+2}.
$$

\step{Partial sum.}
$$
s_n = \left(\frac12 - \frac13\right) + \left(\frac13 - \frac14\right) + \cdots + \left(\frac{1}{n+1} - \frac{1}{n+2}\right) = \frac12 - \frac{1}{n+2}.
$$

\step{Limit.} $\displaystyle \lim_{n\to+\infty} s_n = \lim_{n\to+\infty}\left(\frac12 - \frac{1}{n+2}\right) = \frac12.$
\answer{converges, sum $= \dfrac12$}

\problem{9.}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(2k-1)(2k+1)} = \frac{1}{1\cdot 3} + \frac{1}{3\cdot 5} + \frac{1}{5\cdot 7} + \cdots}

\step{Partial fractions.}
$$
\frac{1}{(2k-1)(2k+1)} = \frac12\left(\frac{1}{2k-1} - \frac{1}{2k+1}\right).
$$

\step{Partial sum.}
$$
s_n = \frac12\left[\left(1 - \frac13\right) + \left(\frac13 - \frac15\right) + \cdots + \left(\frac{1}{2n-1} - \frac{1}{2n+1}\right)\right] = \frac12\left(1 - \frac{1}{2n+1}\right).
$$

\step{Limit.} $\displaystyle \lim_{n\to+\infty} s_n = \frac12(1 - 0) = \frac12.$
\answer{converges, sum $= \dfrac12$}

\problem{10.}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \ln\!\left(\frac{k}{k+1}\right) = \ln\frac12 + \ln\frac23 + \ln\frac34 + \cdots}

\step{Log rule.} $\ln\!\left(\dfrac{k}{k+1}\right) = \ln k - \ln(k+1)$.

\step{Partial sum.}
$$
s_n = (\ln 1 - \ln 2) + (\ln 2 - \ln 3) + \cdots + (\ln n - \ln(n+1)) = \ln 1 - \ln(n+1) = -\ln(n+1).
$$

\step{Limit.} $\displaystyle \lim_{n\to+\infty} s_n = \lim_{n\to+\infty}\big(-\ln(n+1)\big) = -\infty$, so the limit does not exist.
\answer{diverges}

\problem{11.}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{2}{k(k+2)} = \frac{2}{1\cdot 3} + \frac{2}{2\cdot 4} + \frac{2}{3\cdot 5} + \cdots}

\step{Partial fractions.}
$$
\frac{2}{k(k+2)} = \frac1k - \frac{1}{k+2}.
$$

\step{Partial sum.} Now terms cancel \emph{two apart}, so two positive terms survive at the start and two negative terms at the end:
$$
\begin{aligned}
s_n &= \left(1 - \frac13\right) + \left(\frac12 - \frac14\right) + \left(\frac13 - \frac15\right) + \cdots + \left(\frac{1}{n-1} - \frac{1}{n+1}\right) + \left(\frac1n - \frac{1}{n+2}\right) \\
&= 1 + \frac12 - \frac{1}{n+1} - \frac{1}{n+2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

\step{Limit.} $\displaystyle \lim_{n\to+\infty} s_n = 1 + \frac12 - 0 - 0 = \frac32.$
\answer{converges, sum $= \dfrac32$}

\problem{12.}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{4}{k^{2}+4k+3} = \frac{4}{2\cdot 4} + \frac{4}{3\cdot 5} + \frac{4}{4\cdot 6} + \cdots}

\step{Partial fractions.} $k^2 + 4k + 3 = (k+1)(k+3)$, and
$$
\frac{4}{(k+1)(k+3)} = \frac{2}{k+1} - \frac{2}{k+3}.
$$

\step{Partial sum.} Terms cancel two apart:
$$
\begin{aligned}
s_n &= 2\left[\left(\frac12 - \frac14\right) + \left(\frac13 - \frac15\right) + \left(\frac14 - \frac16\right) + \cdots + \left(\frac{1}{n+1} - \frac{1}{n+3}\right)\right] \\
&= 2\left(\frac12 + \frac13 - \frac{1}{n+2} - \frac{1}{n+3}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

\step{Limit.} $\displaystyle \lim_{n\to+\infty} s_n = 2\left(\frac12 + \frac13\right) = 2\cdot\frac56 = \frac53.$
\answer{converges, sum $= \dfrac53$}

\problem{13.}{\frac{1}{4\cdot 5} + \frac{1}{5\cdot 6} + \frac{1}{6\cdot 7} + \cdots + \frac{1}{(k+3)(k+4)} + \cdots}

\step{Sigma form.} This is $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(k+3)(k+4)}$ (check: $k=1$ gives $\frac{1}{4\cdot 5}$).

\step{Partial fractions.}
$$
\frac{1}{(k+3)(k+4)} = \frac{1}{k+3} - \frac{1}{k+4}.
$$

\step{Partial sum.}
$$
s_n = \left(\frac14 - \frac15\right) + \left(\frac15 - \frac16\right) + \cdots + \left(\frac{1}{n+3} - \frac{1}{n+4}\right) = \frac14 - \frac{1}{n+4}.
$$

\step{Limit.} $\displaystyle \lim_{n\to+\infty} s_n = \frac14.$
\answer{converges, sum $= \dfrac14$}

\problem{14.}{\frac{1}{1\cdot 4} + \frac{1}{4\cdot 7} + \frac{1}{7\cdot 10} + \cdots + \frac{1}{(3k-2)(3k+1)} + \cdots}

\step{Sigma form.} This is $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(3k-2)(3k+1)}$ (check: $k=1$ gives $\frac{1}{1\cdot 4}$).

\step{Partial fractions.} The factors differ by $3$, so
$$
\frac{1}{(3k-2)(3k+1)} = \frac13\left(\frac{1}{3k-2} - \frac{1}{3k+1}\right).
$$

\step{Partial sum.}
$$
s_n = \frac13\left[\left(1 - \frac14\right) + \left(\frac14 - \frac17\right) + \cdots + \left(\frac{1}{3n-2} - \frac{1}{3n+1}\right)\right] = \frac13\left(1 - \frac{1}{3n+1}\right).
$$

\step{Limit.} $\displaystyle \lim_{n\to+\infty} s_n = \frac13(1 - 0) = \frac13.$
\answer{converges, sum $= \dfrac13$}
